newsitem.title: GERMANY: Exiles cheer, Bonn cautious after Berlin verdict.
newsitem.headline: Exiles cheer, Bonn cautious after Berlin verdict.

text.p: Exiled Iranians clapped and danced and Bonn officials exercised great caution on Thursday after a Berlin court said Iran's leaders had ordered the killing of three Iranian Kurdish leaders in 1992.

Inside the court, small groups of Iranian exiles burst into applause after hearing the court had sentenced the two main suspects in the case to life in jail and handed down prison sentences between five and 11 years to two others.
Outside, over 1,000 Iranians crowded outside the Berlin court cheered, sang and danced when they heard the news.
Over 100 police were on hand to keep three Iranian exile groups -- Kurds, royalists and followers of the mujahideen resistance group --- away from each other.
A cheer went up from the crowd when an official of the National Council of Resistance of Iran read out a statement from the mujahideen leader Massoud Radjavi.
"For years, there has hardly been any doubt about the role of the criminal mullah regime's leadership in terrorist acts," he said.

"Now a European court has for the first time named (supreme religious leader Ayatollah Ali) Khamenei and (President Akbar Hashemi) Rafsanjani as the masterminds of the attack in Berlin and Tehran's state terrorism."

The court did not identify the Iranian leaders by name but said a Committee for Special Operations to which they belonged had ordered the attack. It specifically noted the president and religious leader were committee members.
In Bonn, the foreign ministry declined any comment until after the court's opinion was read out in full. That could take up to six hours.

A prominent Bonn politician, Free Democrat (FDP) deputy Juergen Moellemann, said Germany should now intensify its controversial "critical dialogue" with Tehran rather than give it up as partners such as the United States have urged.
"A Berlin judge cannot decide how we organise our relations with countries around the world," he said. "If there are problems, one should actually intensify the dialogue."
Germany, Iran's biggest trading partner and most important friend in the West, has said it might have to review relations after the verdict was known.
